lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: The Abbasid Caliphate and the founding of Baghdad
objectives: Explain how the Islamic world grew after the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him
Describe why Baghdad was founded and how it was planned

keywords.def: the leader of the Muslim community and state
the dynasty of caliphs who ruled from Baghdad from AD 750
the capital city founded in AD 762 beside the River Tigris
a developed society with cities, government and culture

starter: Which two groups fought for England in the 800s?
Why is it important to use more than one source?

teach.heading: Bismillah: a great civilisation
bullets: While Britain faced Vikings, Baghdad was thriving
The Islamic world stretched from Spain to Central Asia
We study c. AD 900, over 1,100 years ago
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Compare with Year 5: ask what was happening in Britain around AD 900 (Alfred's successors, Vikings) and show the contrast. Check pupils know the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lived in the 7th century CE.

teach.heading: The Abbasid Caliphate
bullets: The Abbasids came to power in AD 750
Their capital moved east from Damascus
Caliphs ruled a huge empire of many peoples
teach.note: Be accurate and respectful: the Abbasids followed the Umayyads. The empire included Arabs, Persians, Berbers, Christians, Jews and others. Mention that many languages and cultures contributed to the civilisation.

teach.heading: Why Baghdad?
bullets: Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in AD 762
It stood on the River Tigris
Rivers and trade routes made it a rich location
teach.note: Show a map. Ask why a river location helps a city: water, farming, transport, trade. Al-Mansur chose the site carefully, according to historians.

teach.heading: The Round City
bullets: Its walls were about 2.5 kilometres across
The caliph's palace stood at the centre
teach.note: The Round City of Baghdad, also called Madinat al-Salam (City of Peace), had gates facing different directions. Don't claim precise measurements beyond 'about'. Ask what might a round design show about the ruler.

practice: Name two reasons Baghdad was a good place for a capital.
independent: Label a map of the Abbasid Caliphate with Baghdad, Damascus, Cordoba and the River Tigris
Draw the Round City and add four labels
Write 5 sentences explaining why the Abbasids built Baghdad
exit: In which year was Baghdad founded?
Give one reason why a river helps a city grow.
lessons.homework: Ask someone at home how Baghdad or another Islamic city has been important in history and share one fact.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled map outline with a word bank. Stretch: compare Baghdad with London in c. AD 900 using two criteria.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: The House of Wisdom and the love of knowledge
objectives: Explain what the House of Wisdom was
Describe why learning was so important in the Islamic world

keywords.def: the great centre of learning and translation in Baghdad
changing writing from one language into another
a person who has studied a subject deeply
a material for writing, made from plant fibres

starter: Why was Baghdad built on the Tigris?

teach.heading: Seeking knowledge
bullets: The first word revealed to the Prophet was Iqra, read
Muslims were encouraged to seek knowledge
Learning became part of daily life
teach.note: The first revelation, in Surah al-Alaq (96:1), begins with 'Iqra', meaning 'Read' or 'Recite'. Also point out Surah Ta-Ha 20:114: 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.' Cite plainly and with respect.

teach.heading: The House of Wisdom
bullets: Baghdad had a great library and study centre
It grew greatly under Caliph al-Ma'mun (813-833)
teach.note: Historians debate exactly how the institution worked, so say 'a centre of learning and translation'. Avoid overstating specifics. Ask pupils what a library today offers that is the same.

teach.heading: The translation movement
bullets: Greek, Persian and Indian books were translated into Arabic
teach.note: Explain that translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq worked on Greek medical books. Stress the Islamic world not only preserved but improved and added new knowledge.

teach.heading: Paper changes everything
bullets: Paper mills opened in Baghdad around AD 794
More books could be made and sold
teach.note: Knowledge of papermaking came from China. Ask pupils how cheaper paper helps spread knowledge, like printing and the internet later. Booksellers' markets (warraqin) were found in Baghdad.

practice: What was translated in the House of Wisdom?
independent: Draw an inside view of the House of Wisdom with shelves, books, desks and writing tools
Write a diary entry of a scholar visiting Baghdad
Make a flow chart: Greek book, translated into Arabic, new ideas, shared again
exit: Name one thing scholars did in the House of Wisdom.
How did paper help spread knowledge?
lessons.homework: Ask a family member about a scholar or teacher who inspired them and report back one thing they learned.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pictures with key words for the flow chart. Stretch: explain why sharing knowledge across languages leads to new discoveries.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: Scholars and scientists of the golden age
objectives: Describe the work of at least two Muslim scholars
Explain how their ideas still affect us today

keywords.def: a branch of mathematics using letters and symbols for unknown numbers
a mathematician of Baghdad whose book gave algebra its name
a physician and scientist of Baghdad, known as Rhazes in Europe
a place where sick people are cared for by doctors

starter: What was the House of Wisdom?

teach.heading: Al-Khwarizmi
bullets: He worked in the House of Wisdom
His book on solving equations named algebra
teach.note: The word algebra comes from 'al-jabr' in the title of his book. Our word algorithm comes from his name. Show a simple equation, e.g. x + 3 = 10, and ask pupils to solve it: that is algebra.

teach.heading: Numbers we use
bullets: Scholars explained how to use them
They spread to Europe and replaced Roman numerals
teach.note: The numerals developed in India and were explained and spread by scholars including al-Khwarizmi. Ask pupils to compare 1999 with MCMXCIX in Roman numerals.

teach.heading: Al-Razi and medicine
bullets: He wrote many books on medicine
He worked in hospitals in Baghdad and Rayy
teach.note: Al-Razi wrote about measles and smallpox and insisted on careful observation. Hospitals (bimaristans) cared for the sick, including those who couldn't pay. Link to compassion and caring for the sick in Islam.

teach.heading: Building and learning for all
bullets: Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in AD 859
It is one of the oldest universities
Education was open to many people
teach.note: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, was founded by Fatima al-Fihri and is considered one of the world's oldest continually operating universities. Ask: why did she build it? Compare with TGA and school today.

practice: Which word comes from al-Khwarizmi's book title?
Name one thing al-Razi did for medicine.
independent: Make a 'Famous Scholars' fact file for al-Khwarizmi and al-Razi
Write a paragraph: which scholar's work do you think matters most today?
Complete a table of discoveries and how they help us today
lessons.homework: Find one thing in your home or school that uses numbers or maths and explain how algebra or numerals help.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: fact file with images and word bank. Stretch: explain why one scholar's work could not have happened without translated books.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: Trade, markets and legacy: Baghdad compared with Britain
objectives: Describe how trade made Baghdad rich
Compare Baghdad with Britain around AD 900

keywords.def: buying and selling goods
a network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean
a market
to show how two things are different

teach.heading: Baghdad's markets
bullets: Merchants traded silk, spices, paper and glass
Goods came from China, India and Africa
The Tigris and caravans carried goods
teach.note: Bismillah. Show an illustration of a souq. Ask what a visitor to Baghdad might see, smell and hear. Link to trade with Muslim merchants as honest dealers, which is encouraged in Islam.

teach.heading: A city of millions?
bullets: Baghdad was one of the largest cities of its time
Estimates suggest several hundred thousand people
It had mosques, schools, hospitals and gardens
teach.note: Population estimates vary, so say 'possibly 500,000 or more'. Compare to London at this time, which probably had far fewer people. Ask: what does a large population tell us?

teach.heading: Britain around AD 900
bullets: Britain had small towns and villages
teach.note: Revisit Year 5 learning. Be fair: Britain had its own skills, such as metalwork, laws and monasteries. The contrast is about scale of cities and ways of learning, not value of people.

teach.heading: Legacy today
bullets: Algebra, numerals and optics came from this age
Universities, hospitals and libraries grew from it
Many English words come from Arabic
teach.note: English words from Arabic include algebra, algorithm, alcohol, sugar, cotton, magazine and coffee. Ask pupils to find any they use. Close with gratitude and dua for beneficial knowledge.

practice: Name two goods traded in Baghdad.
Give one difference between Baghdad and Britain c. AD 900.
Name one English word that comes from Arabic.
independent: Complete a comparison table: Baghdad and Britain for size, learning, trade
Write a postcard from a merchant arriving in Baghdad
Write a conclusion: What was the most important contribution of Baghdad c. AD 900? Explain why
exit: Name two things that made Baghdad rich.
Name one thing we still use today from this civilisation.
lessons.homework: Make a list of five English words that come from Arabic and find what each means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: comparison table with pictures and sentence stems. Stretch: argue whether 'golden age' is a fair description of Baghdad.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Titanic and polar exploration (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: The Titanic, 1912
lessons.bigQuestion: Could the Titanic disaster have been prevented?
objectives: To understand what happened to the Titanic and why the disaster led to changes
successCriteria: All: order the main events of the Titanic's voyage
Most: explain two causes of the disaster
Some: explain how the disaster changed safety at sea
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: icebergs and the North Atlantic

keywords.def: a long journey by sea
a ship's first journey
a small boat for escaping a sinking ship
a reason something happens
a result of something happening

hook.text: A ship is called 'practically unsinkable'. What might the crew do differently because of that?

islamicLink.text: Allah says that whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all of mankind (al-Ma'idah 5:32). The changes after the Titanic, such as lifeboats for everyone, have saved many lives since. Islam also teaches that we should not be proud and think we are beyond harm.

starter.q: About how much of an iceberg is underwater?

starter.a: Ice breaking off a glacier or ice shelf

teach.heading: The ship
teach.note: Built by Harland and Wolff. Handle this topic calmly: many people died.

teach.heading: The voyage
teach.note: Times are ship's time.

timeline.label: 10 April 1912
timeline.text: Leaves Southampton on its maiden voyage

timeline.label: 14 April, 11.40 pm
timeline.text: Hits an iceberg in the North Atlantic

teach.heading: Why did so many die?
bullets: Lifeboats for only about half on board
Cold water, night, no nearby help
teach.note: About 2,200 people were on board; more than 1,500 died.

items: high speed in an ice field
iceberg hard to see at night

teach.heading: Consequences
bullets: An ice patrol to watch for icebergs
teach.note: A new international safety agreement followed in 1914.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why did more than half the people on board die?
check.why: The lifeboats had room for only about half the people on board.

practice.q: Put in order: Carpathia arrives, hits iceberg, leaves Southampton, sinks.
practice.a: Leaves Southampton, hits iceberg, sinks, Carpathia arrives
practice.model:
Start of the voyage: leaves Southampton.
Then the accident: hits iceberg.
Then: sinks.
Last: rescue by the Carpathia.

practice.q: Give one cause of the high death toll.
Give one change made after the disaster.
practice.a: Lifeboat places for everyone on board

independent.q: Core: Make a timeline of the Titanic's voyage with four dated events.
independent.a: 10 April leaves Southampton; 14 April 11.40 pm hits iceberg; 15 April about 2.20 am sinks; 15 April rescue by the Carpathia
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 10 April 1912, left Southampton on its first voyage.

independent.q: Extend: Write a paragraph: could the disaster have been prevented? Use the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: Yes, partly: slowing down, acting on ice warnings and carrying enough lifeboats would have saved many lives

independent.q: Stretch: Which cause was most important? Explain.
independent.a: Reasoned answer, for example: too few lifeboats, because it decided how many could survive

exit.q: Big question: could the Titanic disaster have been prevented?
exit.a: Partly: by slowing down, acting on ice warnings and carrying enough lifeboats

lessons.homework: Find out what the International Ice Patrol does today.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards to order. EAL: ship, iceberg, sink, rescue. Stretch: research why the wreck was only found in 1985.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Titanic and polar exploration (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Scott and Amundsen: the race to the South Pole
lessons.bigQuestion: Why did Amundsen succeed and Scott's team die?
objectives: To understand the race to the South Pole and the reasons for its different outcomes
successCriteria: All: say who reached the South Pole first and when
Most: compare Scott's and Amundsen's methods
Some: explain the most important reason for the different outcomes

keywords.def: a long journey made for a purpose
someone who travels to find out about new places
a vehicle that slides over snow
a store of food and fuel left for the journey
how something ends

hook.text: If you were racing to the South Pole, would you take dogs, ponies or machines? Why?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches us to plan carefully and then trust Allah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told a man to tie his camel and then trust in Allah (reported by at-Tirmidhi). Good preparation and trust in Allah go together.

teach.heading: Two expeditions
bullets: Both aimed for the South Pole
teach.note: Scott's Terra Nova expedition left Britain in 1910.

teach.heading: Who got there first?
teach.note: Scott's team of five all died on the way back.

timeline.label: March 1912
timeline.text: Scott's party die on the return

teach.heading: Different methods
teach.note: Discuss each point.

teach.heading: Bad luck or bad planning?
bullets: Very cold weather on the return
teach.note: Historians still argue. Both men were brave.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Who reached the South Pole first?
check.why: Amundsen arrived on 14 December 1911, about five weeks before Scott.

practice.q: How many weeks earlier did Amundsen arrive?
practice.a: About five weeks (14 December to 17 January)
practice.model:
14 December to 14 January is one month.
Then 3 more days.
About five weeks.

practice.q: Give one way Amundsen's methods were different.
practice.a: For example: he used skilled dog teams
A store of food and fuel left for the journey

independent.q: Core: Make a comparison table of the two expeditions (leader, country, transport, clothing, outcome).
independent.a: Amundsen: Norway, dogs and skis, fur, reached Pole first and returned safely. Scott: Britain, ponies, motors and man-hauling, wool and windproof cloth, reached Pole second and died on return.
independent.model: Teacher shows row 1: 'Leader and country: Amundsen, Norway; Scott, Britain.'

independent.q: Extend: Write a paragraph explaining why Amundsen succeeded. Use the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: Amundsen succeeded mainly because his dogs and skis were fast and he had many depots, while Scott's team had to haul their own sledges

independent.q: Stretch: Was Scott's failure bad luck or bad planning? Give your view.
independent.a: Reasoned view using weather, illness and planning choices

exit.q: Big question: why did Amundsen succeed and Scott's team die?
exit.a: Amundsen's dogs, skis, fur clothing and depots were better suited; Scott's team faced terrible weather and hauled their own sledges

lessons.homework: Write a short diary entry as an explorer on the polar plateau (describe the place, not people).
lessons.send: SEND: comparison table with picture prompts. EAL: dog, ski, sledge, first, second. Stretch: find out how Amundsen learned his skills from Arctic peoples.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Titanic and polar exploration (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Primary sources from the polar expeditions
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know what happened to Scott's team when none of them came home?
objectives: To understand how primary sources tell us about the polar expeditions and how reliable they are
successCriteria: All: say what a primary source is
Most: say what a source tells us about the expedition
Some: judge how useful and reliable a source is

keywords.def: a source made at the time, by someone involved
a source made later, about the past
a diary kept day by day
can be trusted
helps answer our question

hook.text: If you kept a diary during a dangerous journey, what would you want people to know?

islamicLink.text: Allah tells believers to check news before acting on it (al-Hujurat 49:6). Muslim scholars of hadith built careful methods for checking who reported something and whether they could be trusted. Historians use similar questions with sources.

starter.q: Who reached the South Pole first?

starter.a: A store of food and fuel

teach.heading: Primary or secondary?
teach.note: Amundsen's book was written soon after by someone involved, so it is primary.

teach.heading: Scott's journal
bullets: Found with the tent in November 1912
Describes the cold, hunger and illness
teach.note: We do not need exact quotations: the journal records the weather, the distances and the team's struggles until the end.

teach.heading: Photographs and objects
bullets: Scott's hut still stands at Cape Evans
teach.note: We look at photos of places and objects only.

teach.heading: Asking questions of a source
teach.note: Model with the journal.

steps: Who: Scott, during the journey
Tells us: weather, distances, food, illness
Might leave out: what others felt; he may want to be remembered well
model.answer: Very useful about daily events, but it is one person's view.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Scott's journal was written at the time by someone involved.

practice.q: Is a photograph taken on the expedition primary or secondary?
practice.model:
When was it made? During the expedition.
By someone involved? Yes.
So it is primary.

practice.q: Name one thing Scott's journal tells us.
practice.a: For example: the bad weather, distances travelled, hunger or illness

practice.q: Why might a journal not tell the whole story?
practice.a: It is one person's view and he might leave things out

independent.q: Core: For three sources (journal, photo of the hut, Amundsen's book), write: primary or secondary, what it tells us, one limit.
independent.a: Journal: primary; daily struggles; one person's view. Hut photo: primary or later photo of a primary site; how they lived; does not show feelings. Amundsen's book: primary; his methods; written to tell his success
independent.model: Teacher shows the journal row: 'Primary. Tells us the weather and food problems. Limit: only Scott's view.'

independent.q: Extend: Which source is most useful for the big question? Explain.
independent.a: Scott's journal, because it was written during the return journey and found with the team

independent.q: Stretch: Why might Amundsen's own book praise his methods?
independent.a: He wanted to explain and show his success; writers often present themselves well

exit.a: At the time, by someone involved
options: At the time, by someone involved

exit.q: Big question: how do we know what happened to Scott's team when none of them came home?
exit.a: From primary sources: Scott's journal and the team's records found with the tent, plus photographs and objects

lessons.homework: Interview an older relative about an event they remember and note one thing that makes their account a primary source.
lessons.send: SEND: source cards with captions; primary or secondary stickers. EAL: primary, secondary, diary, photo. Stretch: write one question you would ask Scott if you could.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: From the abacus to the computer
lessons.bigQuestion: Which invention changed the world the most?
objectives: To understand how computing technology developed over time
successCriteria: All: order five inventions on a timeline
Most: explain what each invention did
Some: identify turning points

keywords.def: something new that someone has made or designed
a frame with beads for counting
a line showing events in time order
a moment when things change a lot
the effect something has

hook.text: If you could take one modern invention back 500 years, which would you take?

starter.a: All the steps from raw material to shop
options: All the steps from raw material to shop

teach.heading: Counting tools
bullets: The abacus: used over 2,000 years ago
teach.note: Demonstrate counting on an abacus.

teach.heading: Machines for thinking
bullets: Ada Lovelace wrote a program for one (1843)
teach.note: Colossus at Bletchley Park helped break wartime codes.

teach.heading: Into our pockets
teach.note: Show how big early computers were (photos of machines only).

timeline.text: World Wide Web opens to the public

teach.heading: Turning points
bullets: Something that changed what came after
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Was the World Wide Web a turning point?
steps: Before: computers mostly separate
After: information shared worldwide
So: it changed how people learn, shop and talk

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The abacus is over 2,000 years old.

practice.q: Order: World Wide Web, abacus, printing press, telephone.
practice.a: Abacus, printing press (about 1440), telephone (1876), World Wide Web (1991)
practice.model:
Oldest: abacus.
Then printing press, about 1440.
Then telephone, 1876.
Then World Wide Web, 1991.

independent.q: Core: Make an illustrated technology timeline (objects only, no people) with six inventions, dates and one sentence on each impact.
independent.a: Six correct inventions, dates and impacts
independent.model: Teacher does the abacus entry first.

independent.q: Extend: Circle two turning points and explain why.
independent.a: For example: printing press (books for many), the Web (worldwide sharing)

independent.q: Stretch: Which invention do you think will be next? Why?
independent.a: A reasoned prediction

exit.q: Big question: which invention changed the world the most?
exit.a: A justified choice using its impact

lessons.homework: Ask an older relative what technology they had at your age and compare it with yours.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards to order. EAL: invention words with pictures. Stretch: research how a modern smartphone compares with a 1940s computer.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: The impact of inventions
lessons.bigQuestion: Has every invention made life better?
objectives: To understand how to judge the positive and negative impact of an invention
successCriteria: All: give one good and one bad impact of an invention
Most: use evidence to explain impact
Some: weigh impacts to reach a judgement

keywords.def: the effect something has
good
bad
what happens because of something
facts that support a point

hook.text: Think of something you use every day. What would life be like without it?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said there are two blessings many people are cheated of: good health and free time (Sahih al-Bukhari). Technology can save time or waste it, so we use it with care.

starter.q: The World Wide Web opened to the public in:

starter.a: A moment when things change a lot

teach.heading: The printing press, about 1440
teach.note: Earlier, printing with movable type had been developed in China.

teach.heading: The telephone, 1876
teach.note: Ask: positive or negative?

teach.heading: Weighing impact
teach.note: Use a table.

teach.heading: A judgement
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Was the printing press mostly positive?
steps: Positive: books cheaper, more readers
Negative: false ideas could spread too
Judgement: mostly positive, as learning spread widely

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A negative impact of smartphones is:
check.why: Privacy risks are a harm; the others are benefits.

practice.q: Give one positive and one negative impact of the car.
practice.a: Positive: fast travel; negative: pollution and accidents
practice.model:
Positive: who benefits? Travellers.
Negative: what harm? Fumes and accidents.
Now I have both sides.

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write a balanced paragraph on one invention: positive impact, negative impact, judgement. Starter: 'One positive impact of ... was ...'
independent.a: Balanced paragraph with evidence and a judgement
independent.model: Teacher writes the printing press paragraph first.

independent.q: Extend: Compare the impact of two inventions. Which was greater?
independent.a: A justified comparison

independent.q: Stretch: How should Muslims use technology well?
independent.a: With good intentions, for knowledge and family, without wasting time or harming others

exit.q: Big question: has every invention made life better?
exit.a: No: most have positives and negatives; how we use them matters

lessons.homework: Survey your family: which invention could they not live without? Tally the answers.
lessons.send: SEND: impact table with sentence starters. EAL: good, bad, effect with pictures. Stretch: research the impact of the printing press on the Islamic world (printing arrived later there).

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a book written in Baghdad 1,200 years ago be in your maths lessons today?
objectives: To understand al-Khwarizmi's contribution to mathematics and computing
successCriteria: All: say who al-Khwarizmi was
Most: explain where 'algebra' and 'algorithm' come from
Some: explain why his work matters to computing
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Muslim contributions to world knowledge

keywords.def: maths using letters for unknown numbers
a set of steps to solve a problem
a person who studies deeply
a centre of learning in Baghdad
symbols for numbers

hook.text: Is it fair that we call our numbers 'Arabic numerals'? Where do you think they came from?

islamicLink.text: Islam praises those who seek knowledge: Allah asks, are those who know equal to those who do not know? (Az-Zumar 39:9). Scholars like al-Khwarizmi saw learning about numbers as part of understanding Allah's ordered creation.

starter.q: Which came first: the printing press or the abacus?
Baghdad is in which modern country?

teach.heading: Who was al-Khwarizmi?
bullets: Worked in the House of Wisdom, Baghdad
teach.note: Abbasid caliphs supported scholars.

teach.heading: Algebra
teach.note: He wrote problems in words; letters came later.

model.problem: A number plus 5 makes 12. What is the number?
steps: Write it: ? + 5 = 12
Take 5 from both sides

teach.heading: Numbers and algorithms
teach.note: Computers follow algorithms: steps in order.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Latin versions of his name gave 'algorismus', then 'algorithm'.

practice.q: Write a 4-step algorithm for making wudu's first steps.
practice.a: For example: intention; say bismillah; wash hands three times; rinse mouth three times

independent.q: Core: Make a fact file on al-Khwarizmi: who, when, where, three contributions, why they matter today.
independent.a: Accurate fact file

independent.q: Extend: Solve three 'al-jabr' problems and write the steps.
independent.a: For example: ? + 14 = 30, so ? = 16

independent.q: Stretch: Explain the link between al-Khwarizmi and computer programs.
independent.a: Programs are algorithms: step-by-step instructions, a word from his name

exit.q: Big question: how is a book from Baghdad in your maths lessons?
exit.a: Al-Khwarizmi's algebra and numerals spread through translation to Europe and are still taught

lessons.homework: Write an algorithm (numbered steps) for a task at home, such as making tea, and test it with a family member.
lessons.send: SEND: fact file headings and word bank. EAL: algebra, algorithm with examples. Stretch: write your own al-jabr word problem.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Ibn al-Haytham and optics
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we see? Does light go into our eyes or come out of them?
objectives: To understand how Ibn al-Haytham changed ideas about light and how science is done
successCriteria: All: say who Ibn al-Haytham was
Most: explain his idea about how we see
Some: explain why his experiments mattered
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: studying light as a sign of Allah's creation

keywords.def: the science of light and sight
a test to find out if an idea is true
a dark room or box where light through a small hole makes an image
facts that support an idea
a planned way of doing something

hook.text: Some ancient thinkers said our eyes send out rays to see. How could you test that idea?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth (An-Nur 24:35). Muslim scholars studied light and sight carefully, seeing science as a way to understand Allah's creation.

starter.q: The House of Wisdom was in:

teach.heading: Who was Ibn al-Haytham?
teach.note: Link to Year 6 science: light.

teach.heading: How we see
bullets: Old idea: rays came out of the eye
His idea: light enters the eye
Light bounces off objects into our eyes
teach.note: This is what we still teach today.

misconception.wrong: Our eyes send out rays to see things
misconception.right: Light from a source bounces off objects and enters our eyes

teach.heading: Testing ideas
teach.note: He studied the camera obscura: light through a small hole makes an upside-down image.

teach.heading: Explaining his importance
teach.note: Model.

steps: Point: he showed light enters the eye
Evidence: experiments in the Book of Optics
Explain: he helped start testing ideas by experiment
model.answer: He changed both what we know about light and how science is done

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Ibn al-Haytham showed that we see because:
check.why: Light bounces off objects into our eyes.

practice.q: Why can we not see in a completely dark room?
practice.a: No light to bounce off objects into our eyes
practice.model:
Seeing needs light.
In the dark there is no light.
Nothing bounces into our eyes.
So we cannot see.

independent.q: Core: Make a pinhole viewer (camera obscura) from a box or tube with an adult, OR complete the diagram sheet, then write what you observed and how it supports his idea. Written guide on the sheet.
independent.a: An upside-down image observed or a correct ray diagram, with an explanation
independent.model: Teacher shows a pinhole viewer on camera and draws the ray diagram.

independent.q: Extend: Compare Ibn al-Haytham and al-Khwarizmi: what did they share?
independent.a: Both worked in the Muslim world, used careful methods and influenced later science

independent.q: Stretch: Why does testing matter more than just trusting old books?
independent.a: Evidence shows if an idea is true; old ideas can be wrong

exit.q: Big question: how do we see?
exit.a: Light from a source bounces off objects and enters our eyes

lessons.homework: Show your pinhole viewer to your family and explain Ibn al-Haytham's idea.
lessons.send: SEND: diagram sheet with arrows to complete. EAL: light, eye, hole with pictures. Stretch: research how his work was translated into Latin. Safety: never look at the Sun through the viewer; an adult helps with sharp tools.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 6 curriculum map and history and geography long-term plans 2023-24 (Tomorrow's World); TGA Year 6 pack, History and geography, Spring 2 (CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Pinhole viewer written guide and ray diagram sheet (portal printable)
A shoebox or kitchen-roll tube, foil, tracing paper, tape, a pin (with an adult)
Year 6 science light lessons for cross-reference

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Debate preparation: does technology make the world better?
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you argue well for a side you do not agree with?
objectives: To understand how to build a strong argument with evidence for a debate
successCriteria: All: give one argument with evidence
Most: plan arguments for your side
Some: predict and answer the other side's points
lessons.crossCurricular: English: spoken language and persuasive speech

keywords.def: a formal discussion where two sides argue
a reason given to support a view
facts that support a point
answering the other side's point
the statement being debated

hook.text: Name one technology that has made your life better and one that has made it worse.

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us to argue in the way that is best (An-Nahl 16:125). In a debate we challenge ideas, never insult people.

starter.q: Name one invention and its date.
starter.a: For example: telephone 1876; World Wide Web 1991

teach.heading: The motion
teach.note: Explain the format and debate rules (adab: respect, no interrupting).

teach.heading: Building arguments
teach.note: Model one.

steps: Point: technology saves lives
Evidence: medical machines and phones to call for help
Explain: people survive illnesses and accidents
model.answer: A PEE argument for the motion

teach.heading: Rebuttal
teach.note: Model a rebuttal: 'They say screens waste time; however, used well, they help us learn.'

teach.heading: Debate etiquette
teach.note: Islamic adab of disagreement: speak in the best way.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: A rebuttal answers the other team's argument.

practice.q: Write one argument AGAINST the motion with evidence.
practice.a: For example: screens can harm sleep and attention; e-waste harms the environment
practice.model:
Point: technology can harm health.
Evidence: too much screen time disturbs sleep.
Explain: tired children learn less.

independent.q: Core: In a breakout group, plan three arguments and two rebuttals for your side on the debate planning sheet.
independent.a: Three PEE arguments and two rebuttals
independent.model: Teacher plans the first argument with the class.

independent.q: Extend: Write a 30-second opening speech.
independent.a: A clear opening with your best argument

independent.q: Stretch: Prepare a closing summary that answers the other side.
independent.a: A summary including a rebuttal

exit.q: Big question: can you argue well for a side you disagree with?
exit.a: Yes, by using evidence and understanding the other view

lessons.homework: Practise your opening speech aloud to your family; time it at 30 seconds.
lessons.send: SEND: argument cards to choose from. EAL: debate phrases bank. Stretch: be the chair and plan questions.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 6 curriculum map and history and geography long-term plans 2023-24 (Tomorrow's World); TGA Year 6 pack, History and geography, Spring 2 (CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Debate planning sheet and phrase bank (portal printable)
Teams breakout rooms
Notes from earlier technology and geography lessons

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The history of technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: The debate and our unit review
lessons.bigQuestion: Does technology make the world better?
objectives: To understand how to present, answer and judge arguments in a debate, and review the unit
successCriteria: All: speak once in the debate
Most: use evidence from the unit
Some: rebut the other side and reach a final judgement

keywords.def: a formal discussion where two sides argue
facts that support a point
answering the other side's point
a decision based on reasons
look back at what we learned

hook.text: Before the debate starts: which side do you think will win? Will you change your mind?

starter.q: Who wrote the Book of Optics?

teach.heading: Debate order
teach.note: Teacher chairs; mics on in turn.

teach.heading: Using the unit
teach.note: Encourage evidence from geography lessons too.

teach.heading: Judging
bullets: Which side used the best evidence?
teach.note: Model a judgement.

steps: List the strongest point on each side
Check the evidence
Decide which was more convincing

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

practice.q: Give the strongest point you heard from the other side.
practice.a: Any accurate point from the debate
practice.model:
Think: which point was hardest to answer?
Write it down.
Say why it was strong.

independent.q: Core: Take part in the debate: deliver your planned points and at least one rebuttal (assessed debate contribution).
independent.a: Clear points with evidence; respectful turn-taking
independent.model: Teacher, as chair, models the first opening speech format.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, write your final judgement in one paragraph.
independent.a: A balanced judgement with evidence from both sides

exit.q: A good debate judge decides on:
Big question: does technology make the world better?
exit.a: A reasoned judgement: often better when used wisely, with real risks to manage

lessons.homework: Tell your family the result of the debate and the best argument from each side.
lessons.send: SEND: a prepared card to read in the debate. EAL: phrase bank. Stretch: chair part of the debate. Respectful disagreement throughout.
